additions.reason: The Rebbe states: 'כִּי כַּעַס, שֶׁהִיא הֶפֶךְ הָרַחֲמָנוּת, הוּא מֵחֲמַת כְּסִילוּת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: כַּעַס בְּחֵיק כְּסִילִים יָנוּחַ' (Kohelet 7:9). The structure is: anger = foolishness, compassion = daas. This means כְּסִילוּת (foolishness) is the negative pole of דַּעַת in this Torah — it is the anti-daas, the state of weekdays without Shabbat-light. While this is stated primarily through a verse citation rather than an explicit 'X הוא בחינת Y', the verse-proof 'כַּעַס בְּחֵיק כְּסִילִים יָנוּחַ' establishes כְּסִילוּת as the domain of anger and the absence of daas. In Torah #119's framework, the two poles are: Shabbat/daas/compassion (good) vs. weekday-folly/anger/no-compassion (evil). כְּסִילוּת is the bechina node of that evil pole. It belongs in Package 1 as the evil mirror of דַּעַת within the same package — though it has the opposite polarity, it is the explicit counterpart concept named by the Torah for daas.

additions.reason: The Rebbe explicitly names כַּעַס as 'הֶפֶךְ הָרַחֲמָנוּת' — the direct opposite of compassion. Compassion is the fruit of daas (Shabbat). Therefore anger is the fruit of the absence of daas — i.e., the fruit of כְּסִילוּת (foolishness). In this Torah's binary structure, כַּעַס is the evil counterpart to רַחֲמָנוּת and the behavioral marker of those without daas. The verse 'כַּעַס בְּחֵיק כְּסִילִים יָנוּחַ' establishes the bechina: anger = foolishness = anti-daas. This node forms a bechina pair with כְּסִילוּת and together they represent the negative pole of Torah #119's conceptual axis.
